---
title: "Testing against a threshold"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")
```

```{r setup}
library(MMSpower)
```

Some surveillance questions are not "what is the prevalence?" but "is it
above a level that calls for action?". The standard example is *pfhrp2/3*
gene deletions. Parasites lacking these genes are missed by HRP2-based
rapid diagnostic tests, and WHO recommends switching to a different test
once the prevalence of deletions causing false-negative results is above
5%. A programme suspects deletions are around 10% in one region and wants
a survey that will show prevalence is above 5% if that is true.

`design_threshold()` gives the sample size, and `test_threshold()` analyses
the data. Both use an exact binomial test by default.

## How many samples?

Power is the chance that the survey correctly shows prevalence is above the
threshold, when the true prevalence is above it. The usual target is 80%.
Take the simplest case first: no clustering, a perfect test, a 5% threshold,
and an expected prevalence of 10%:

```{r}
d0 <- design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.10)
d0
```

So `r d0$n` samples are needed. `power` is the power this rounded design
actually achieves,
`r round(d0$power, 3)`, just above the 0.8 target. The
gap between the expected prevalence and the threshold is what matters most:
the closer the true prevalence is to 5%, the harder it is to tell apart from
5%, and the sample size grows quickly.

## Why power is a saw-tooth

With an exact test, power does not always go up when samples are added.
The test declares "above 5%" only once the number of positive samples
reaches a cut-off. That cut-off is a whole number, so as the sample size
grows it holds steady and then steps up by one; each step makes "above 5%"
harder to reach, so power dips a little before climbing again. The plot
shows exact power for every sample size from 2 to 300, for a true prevalence
of 10% against the 5% threshold.

```{r}
n_grid <- 2:300
pw <- numeric(length(n_grid))
for (i in seq_along(n_grid)) {
  pw[i] <- design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.10,
                            n_sites = 1, n_per_site = n_grid[i])$power
}
n_first <- min(n_grid[pw >= 0.8])

par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1), las = 1, bty = "l")
plot(n_grid, pw, type = "l", lwd = 1.5, col = "#1B2A41", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Sample size", ylab = "Power")
abline(h = 0.8, lty = 2, col = "#6B7280")
abline(v = c(n_first, d0$n), col = c("#6B7280", "#C0392B"), lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c(paste("First n with 80% power:", n_first),
                  paste("n returned:", d0$n)),
       col = c("#6B7280", "#C0392B"), lwd = 2)
```

Power first reaches 80% at n = `r n_first`, but at several larger sample
sizes it falls back below 80%. `design_threshold()` returns `r d0$n`, the
smallest sample size from which power **never** drops back below the
target. This is the safe choice: in the field, a few samples are always
lost or added (failed extractions, an extra day at a site), and with the
returned size none of this can push the study below 80% power.

## Showing prevalence is below a threshold

The question can also run the other way. After a switch of test, a
programme may want to confirm that deletions are now **below** 5%. Use
`alternative = "less"`, with the expected prevalence below the threshold:

```{r}
design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.02, alternative = "less")$n
```

The burden of proof is reversed. A one-sided test only concludes what it
sets out to show when the evidence is strong, so failing to show prevalence
is *above* 5% is not the same as showing it is *below* 5%, the data may
simply be inconclusive. Each direction is a separate test with its own
sample size.

## An imperfect test

The assay used to call a deletion is not perfect. Suppose it detects 90% of
true deletions (sensitivity) and correctly clears 98% of true non-deletions
(specificity):

```{r}
d_test <- design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.10,
                           sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.98)
d_test$n
```

The sample size rises from `r d0$n` to `r d_test$n`. Power depends on the
gap between the prevalence (10%) and the threshold (5%): a smaller gap needs
more samples. An imperfect test measures both on the scale of what would
test positive, which pulls 10% and 5% closer together by a factor of
$Se + Sp - 1$, so the gap shrinks and more samples are needed.

## Clustering

In practice samples come from sites, and, as in the
[Estimating prevalence](tutorial-prevalence.html) tutorial, an ICC above 0
means more samples are needed. With 20 samples
per site and an ICC of 0.05, solve for the number of sites:

```{r}
d_ps <- design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.10,
                         n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_ps
```

This needs `r d_ps$n_sites` sites of 20 samples, `r d_ps$n` in total,
against the `r d0$n` a simple random sample would need.

Or fix the number of sites at 15 and solve for the samples per site:

```{r}
d_ns <- design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.10,
                         n_sites = 15, icc = 0.05)
d_ns
```

This needs `r d_ns$n_per_site` samples per site, `r d_ns$n` in total. Both
examples report the same `n_eff`, `r d_ps$n_eff`.

To find the power of a design you already have, give the full design and
leave out `power`:

```{r}
p15 <- design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.10,
                        n_sites = 15, n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)$power
p15
```

Fifteen sites of 20 samples give a power of `r round(p15, 2)`, short of the
0.80 target: this design is a little too small, which is why solving for the
number of sites above returned `r d_ps$n_sites` sites.

As with
`design_precision()`, too few sites make the target unreachable, because
each site is worth at most $1/\text{ICC}$ independent samples:

```{r, error = TRUE}
design_threshold(threshold = 0.05, prevalence = 0.10,
                 n_sites = 8, icc = 0.05)
```

These sample sizes assume the data will be analysed with the same ICC used
to design them (0.05). If the analysis instead estimates the ICC and it
comes out higher, the effective sample size is smaller and the true power
falls below the target.

## Analysing the data

The survey is now complete: 19 sites of 20 samples. We want to assess
whether the prevalence is above the 5% threshold. `test_threshold()` takes
the number of samples with a deletion (`x`) and the number tested (`n`) at
each site:

```{r}
x <- c(0, 4, 1, 0, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 6, 0, 2, 4, 0, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2)
n <- rep(20, 19)
res <- test_threshold(x, n, threshold = 0.05)
res
```

The estimated prevalence is `r round(100 * res$prevalence, 1)`%, and the
p-value is `r format(signif(res$p_value, 2), scientific = FALSE)`, so `reject` is `r res$reject`:
the data show prevalence is above 5%. The ICC has been estimated from the
sites (`r round(res$icc, 3)`), and the test is based on the effective
sample size `n_eff` rather than the `r sum(n)` samples tested. Because the
ICC was estimated, the test also allows for the uncertainty in that
estimate, using `df` (the number of sites minus one): with few sites it
becomes more cautious.

### The one-sided interval

Because the question is one-sided ("is it above 5%?"), the interval is
one-sided too: it runs from `ci_lower` = `r round(100 * res$ci_lower, 1)`%
up to 100%. It holds every threshold the test would not reject, so
`reject` is `TRUE` exactly when the threshold lies outside the interval.
Here 5% is below `ci_lower`, which agrees with the test.

### Exact or Wald?

The Wald test uses a normal approximation in place of the exact test's
binomial distribution when the ICC is supplied. When the ICC is estimated,
it uses a t distribution with `df` (sites minus one) instead of the normal,
to allow for the uncertainty in the estimated clustering. `res_wald` is the
previous analysis redone with the Wald method; compare its p-value and lower
bound with the exact test's (`res`):

```{r}
res_wald <- test_threshold(x, n, threshold = 0.05, method = "wald")
rbind(exact = unlist(res[c("p_value", "ci_lower")]),
      wald  = unlist(res_wald[c("p_value", "ci_lower")]))
```

With this much data the two reach the same conclusion, with similar lower
bounds, although their p-values differ. They can differ especially with small samples or a
prevalence near 0, which is common for deletion surveys. An extreme case is
a single site of 20 samples with no deletions, tested for being below 5%:

```{r}
exact <- test_threshold(0, 20, threshold = 0.05, alternative = "less")
wald  <- test_threshold(0, 20, threshold = 0.05, alternative = "less",
                        method = "wald")
rbind(exact = unlist(exact[c("p_value", "reject", "ci_upper")]),
      wald  = unlist(wald[c("p_value", "reject", "ci_upper")]))
```

With no positives, the Wald standard error is 0, so the Wald interval has
zero width and any threshold above 0 is rejected: it claims proof that
prevalence is below 5% from just 20 samples. The exact test does not, and
its interval runs up to `r round(100 * exact$ci_upper, 1)`%. This is why
`"exact"` is the default.

### Supplying the ICC

Previously the ICC was estimated from the data. It can also be supplied, for
example from earlier studies; here we assume an ICC of 0.05:

```{r}
res_icc <- test_threshold(x, n, threshold = 0.05, icc = 0.05)
round(unlist(res_icc), 4)
```

The supplied ICC appears as `icc` in the output, and `df` is now `Inf`: a
known ICC carries no uncertainty, so the test adds no extra caution for it.
When the ICC was estimated, `df` was the number of sites minus one, which
made the test more cautious, and `n_eff` differs too because it depends on
the ICC.

Supplying the ICC or estimating it makes no difference to the false-alarm
rate: either way the test wrongly declares "above 5%" at most 5% of the
time. What changes is power. The caution the test takes for an uncertain
estimated ICC, the finite `df` above, costs power, so a real excess is
harder to detect. A trustworthy ICC from earlier surveys avoids that cost.

## When to use DRpower instead

For *pfhrp2/3* deletion surveys with several sites and an unknown ICC,
consider the [DRpower](https://mrc-ide.github.io/DRpower/) package instead.
DRpower fits a Bayesian beta-binomial model that estimates the prevalence
and the ICC together, rather than fixing the ICC or plugging in a single
estimate. It carries the uncertainty about the ICC through to the
prevalence, and answers the threshold question directly, from the posterior
probability that prevalence is above 5%. The pay-off is more power,
especially with few sites; the cost is more false alarms when the true
prevalence is close to the threshold.

MMSpower is the better choice when you can supply the ICC from earlier
surveys, or when you want a standard frequentist test whose false-alarm rate
is held at or below the stated level.
